pages.h1: Can an RTX 4090 Run Llama 3 70B in Q4?
pages.title: Llama 3 70B Q4 on an RTX 4090 — VRAM Verdict & Calculator
pages.description: A 70B model at Q4_K_M needs about 42 GB of weights. An RTX 4090 has 24 GB. See the exact shortfall, what fits instead, and calculate your own context length.
pages.intro: Llama 3.3 70B at Q4_K_M stores roughly 4.83 bits per weight, which works out to about 42.3 GB of model weights before you allocate a single token of KV cache. An RTX 4090 offers 24 GB of VRAM, of which around 21.6 GB is realistically addressable by llama.cpp or vLLM after the display and CUDA context take their share.
pages.verdict: No. A single RTX 4090 cannot hold 70B at Q4 even with a 2K context and KV cache quantization — the weights alone are about twice the card's capacity. The practical options are 32B at Q5 (about 23 GB, tight), 70B at Q2 (about 23 GB, noticeably degraded), or two 24 GB cards in tensor parallel.

faq.q: What is the largest model an RTX 4090 can run?
faq.a: Around 32B parameters at Q4_K_M (about 19.3 GB) with a 8K–16K context, or 32B at Q5_K_M (about 22.7 GB) if you keep the context near 4K. Above that you are paging weights over PCIe, and throughput collapses from roughly 15 tokens/sec to under 3.

faq.q: Would Q2_K make 70B fit on one 4090?
faq.a: Barely. Q2_K lands near 23 GB for the weights, leaving no room for KV cache at usable context lengths, and 2-bit quantization visibly degrades instruction following on 70B models. It is a demo, not a workflow.

faq.q: How much faster is dual 4090 than a single 4090 for 70B?
faq.a: Two cards give you a 48 GB pool, enough for 70B Q4 with a 8K context. Expect roughly 8–11 tokens/sec in tensor parallel over PCIe, versus 0 for a single card that cannot load the model at all.

pages.h1: DeepSeek R1 Local VRAM & GPU Requirements
pages.title: DeepSeek R1 Local VRAM Requirements Calculator (671B MoE)
pages.description: DeepSeek R1 is a 671B mixture-of-experts model. Calculate the real memory requirement at Q4, Q8 and FP16, plus the KV cache overhead for long reasoning traces.
pages.intro: DeepSeek R1 activates roughly 37B of its 671B parameters per token, which keeps compute cost reasonable but does not shrink the memory footprint: every expert must be resident in memory. At Q4_K_M the weights alone are about 405 GB, and long chain-of-thought traces push the KV cache into the tens of gigabytes.
pages.verdict: Not on any single consumer device. The smallest realistic local setup is a 512 GB unified-memory Mac Studio at Q2–Q3 for slow single-stream use, or a multi-node server. For most teams the hosted API, priced per token, is dramatically cheaper than the hardware required to run R1 locally.

faq.q: Does MoE reduce the memory requirement of DeepSeek R1?
faq.a: No. Sparsity reduces FLOPs per token, not storage. All 671B parameters must be available, so the memory requirement is identical to a dense model of the same size. Only the compute and the achievable tokens/sec improve.

faq.q: Why does a reasoning model need so much KV cache?
faq.a: Chain-of-thought generation can produce 10k–30k tokens before the final answer. KV cache scales linearly with total context, so a 32K reasoning trace at 61 layers and 576-dim KV heads costs roughly 4.5 GB on its own, on top of the weights.

faq.q: Are there smaller DeepSeek R1 distills?
faq.a: Yes. The R1 distills run from 1.5B to 70B and are dense models fine-tuned on R1 traces. A 32B distill at Q4 fits a single 24 GB card and is the practical local option for most developers.

pages.h1: Llama 3.1 8B on an RTX 3060 12GB
pages.title: Llama 3.1 8B VRAM on an RTX 3060 12GB — Speed & Context Limits
pages.description: Llama 3.1 8B at Q4_K_M needs about 5 GB. See how much context an RTX 3060 12GB can support and what tokens/sec to expect from 360 GB/s of bandwidth.
pages.intro: Llama 3.1 8B is a 32-layer dense model with grouped-query attention (8 KV heads). At Q4_K_M it occupies roughly 4.8 GB, and its KV cache costs about 0.125 MB per token — meaning a full 128K context would add 16 GB, far more than the card has.
pages.verdict: Yes, comfortably. On an RTX 3060 12GB you can run 8B at Q4_K_M with a 16K–32K context at roughly 30–38 tokens/sec, which is a genuinely usable local assistant. Quality is best served by spending the spare VRAM on context and a higher quant rather than a larger model.

faq.q: Is Q5_K_M worth it on a 12GB card for 8B?
faq.a: Yes. Q5_K_M costs about 5.7 GB instead of 4.8 GB and leaves room for a 16K context on a 12GB card. The quality gain is small but real, especially on code and non-English text.

faq.q: Why is my tokens/sec lower than the estimate?
faq.a: The estimate uses peak memory bandwidth. Real throughput drops with prompt processing, PCIe weight transfers if part of the model is offloaded to CPU, small batch sizes, and power-limited laptop variants of the same GPU.

faq.q: Can I run two models at once?
faq.a: An 8B Q4 plus a small embedding model fits, but two 8B instances will not both fit in 12 GB at useful context. Run one inference server and route requests to it instead.

pages.h1: Qwen 2.5 32B on an RTX 3090 24GB
pages.title: Qwen 2.5 32B VRAM on an RTX 3090 — Q4 vs Q5 Comparison
pages.description: 32B at Q4_K_M is about 19 GB; at Q5_K_M it is about 23 GB. Find out which quantization an RTX 3090 can actually run with a usable context window.
pages.intro: Qwen 2.5 32B has 64 layers and 8 KV heads, so its KV cache costs about 0.25 MB per token — 8 GB at a 32K context. That overhead is what decides between Q4 and Q5 on a 24 GB card, not the weights alone.
pages.verdict: Conditional. Q4_K_M fits with roughly 4 GB left for a 16K context, which is the right balance for an RTX 3090. Q5_K_M puts you at the ceiling: it works at 4K–8K context, but any longer prompt forces CPU offload and drops throughput sharply.

faq.q: What context length can an RTX 3090 support with 32B Q4?
faq.a: Around 16K tokens once you reserve about 1.5 GB for activations. At 32K the KV cache alone adds 8 GB and the model no longer fits without offloading.

faq.q: Does KV cache quantization help?
faq.a: Yes. Storing the KV cache at Q8 halves its footprint with negligible quality impact, which buys roughly 8K extra context on this configuration.

faq.q: How fast is 32B Q4 on a 3090?
faq.a: About 20 tokens/sec at the theoretical bandwidth limit, typically 15–18 in practice, which is comfortable for chat and single-agent coding.

pages.h1: Mistral 7B on a 16GB GPU: Context & Quantization Guide
pages.title: Mistral 7B VRAM Requirements on a 16GB GPU
pages.description: Mistral 7B needs about 4.4 GB at Q4_K_M. See how much context a 16GB card unlocks and whether Q6_K is worth the extra memory.
pages.intro: Mistral 7B is a 32-layer model with 8 KV heads, so its KV cache is roughly 0.125 MB per token. On a 16GB card, the weights are almost free and the real budget question becomes how much context and how many concurrent requests you want to serve.
pages.verdict: Yes, with room to spare. Mistral 7B at Q6_K uses about 5.9 GB, leaving roughly 8.5 GB on a 16GB card — enough for a 32K context or four concurrent 8K sessions. This is one of the few configurations where higher quantization costs you nothing practical.

faq.q: Is 16GB enough for Mistral 7B with a 32K context?
faq.a: Yes. Weights at Q6_K take about 5.9 GB and a 32K KV cache about 4 GB, leaving several gigabytes for activations and batching.

faq.q: Should I use FP16 on a 16GB card?
faq.a: Only if you can live with a short context. FP16 doubles the weights to about 14.4 GB, which leaves almost nothing for KV cache on a 16GB card and no headroom for the display.

faq.q: How many concurrent users can it serve?
faq.a: Roughly four to six at 8K context with continuous batching, but throughput per request falls as the batch grows because decoding is bandwidth bound.

pages.h1: Can a 192GB Mac Studio Run Llama 3.1 405B?
pages.title: Llama 3.1 405B on a 192GB Mac Studio — Real Memory Math
pages.description: 405B at Q4_K_M is about 245 GB. A 192GB Mac Studio M3 Ultra gives you roughly 138 GB usable. See what actually fits.
pages.intro: Llama 3.1 405B is a dense 126-layer model. Even at 2-bit quantization it needs about 132 GB, which is right at the practical limit of a 192GB Mac Studio once macOS reserves memory and the KV cache is allocated.
pages.verdict: No at Q4 — 245 GB of weights against roughly 138 GB usable. A 192GB Mac Studio can hold 405B at 2-bit (about 132 GB) with a very short context, or a 70B model at Q8 (about 74 GB) with a generous 32K context, which is the far better use of the machine.

faq.q: How much unified memory can a model actually use on macOS?
faq.a: macOS reserves a share for the system and GPU driver. We model roughly 70–72% as addressable by the inference process, so a 192GB machine gives about 138 GB.

faq.q: What is the largest model that fits in 192GB?
faq.a: About 405B at 2-bit, or 70B at Q8 / 120B-class MoE at Q4 with a useful context. Above that, expect heavy swap and single-digit token rates.

faq.q: Is a Mac Studio faster than a multi-GPU server for large models?
faq.a: No. At 819 GB/s the M3 Ultra has far less bandwidth than an H100 (3350 GB/s) or even two 4090s. Its advantage is capacity per watt and per dollar, not tokens/sec.

pages.h1: Qwen 2.5 14B on an RTX 4070 Ti Super 16GB
pages.title: Qwen 2.5 14B VRAM & Context Guide (RTX 4070 Ti Super)
pages.description: 14B at Q6_K is about 11.5 GB. With a 32K context the KV cache adds another 6.3 GB. See where the limit lands on a 16GB card.
pages.intro: Qwen 2.5 14B has 48 layers with 8 KV heads, giving a relatively heavy KV cache of about 0.19 MB per token. That makes long context, not the weights, the binding constraint on a 16GB card.
pages.verdict: Tight at 32K, comfortable at 8K. Q6_K plus an 8K context uses about 13 GB of the roughly 14.4 GB usable and runs fast thanks to 672 GB/s of bandwidth. Push to 32K and you need Q4_K_M to stay on the GPU.

faq.q: Why does 14B use more KV cache than 32B in some cases?
faq.a: KV cache depends on layer count and KV head configuration, not parameter count alone. 14B has 48 layers at 8 KV heads while some 32B checkpoints use fewer or smaller KV heads.

faq.q: Does the 4070 Ti Super beat a 3090 for 14B?
faq.a: No. The 3090 has 936 GB/s versus 672 GB/s, so it decodes faster and has 8 GB more capacity. The 4070 Ti Super wins on power efficiency and purchase price.

faq.q: What is the max context I can run?
faq.a: At Q4_K_M, roughly 32K with KV cache quantization; at Q6_K, roughly 12K before you must offload layers to the CPU.

pages.h1: Llama 3.3 70B on Dual RTX 3090 (48GB)
pages.title: Llama 3.3 70B on Dual RTX 3090 — Does 48GB Fit Q4?
pages.description: 70B at Q4_K_M needs about 42 GB of weights; two 3090s give 43 GB usable. See what context fits and the tokens/sec to expect over PCIe.
pages.intro: Two RTX 3090s give a 48 GB pool at 936 GB/s of bandwidth. Llama 3.3 70B at Q4_K_M consumes about 42.3 GB of that, and its 80-layer, 8-KV-head architecture adds about 2.6 GB at an 8K context.
pages.verdict: Yes, just. Q4_K_M with an 8K context fits in about 46.5 GB against 43.2 GB usable, so it is genuinely tight — expect to run with KV cache quantization at Q8, or keep the context near 4K. Throughput lands around 10–12 tokens/sec.

faq.q: Is NVLink required for dual 3090 inference?
faq.a: No, but it helps. Without NVLink, tensor-parallel layers exchange activations over PCIe every token, which costs a few tokens/sec at 70B. Pipeline parallelism over PCIe is slower still.

faq.q: What quantization do dual 3090s allow for 70B?
faq.a: Q4_K_M with a short context, or Q3-class quantization with a longer one. Q5_K_M at about 49.7 GB exceeds the 43 GB usable pool and forces CPU offload.

faq.q: Dual 3090 or one RTX 5090 for 70B?
faq.a: Neither fits 70B cleanly. The 5090 has 32 GB at much higher bandwidth, so it runs 32B far faster; dual 3090s give you the capacity to load 70B at a modest speed.

pages.h1: Llama 3.3 70B at Q8 on an A100 80GB
pages.title: Llama 3.3 70B Q8 on A100 80GB — Fit, Context & Throughput
pages.description: 70B at Q8_0 is about 74 GB of weights on an 80GB A100. See the exact context headroom and tokens/sec at 2039 GB/s.
pages.intro: Q8_0 is effectively lossless and costs about 74.4 GB for a 70B model. On an 80GB A100 with roughly 76 GB usable, that leaves only a small window for KV cache — which matters because 70B's 80 layers produce about 0.31 MB of cache per token.
pages.verdict: Tight but viable. Q8_0 with a 4K context fits in about 75.7 GB; anything beyond 8K requires KV cache quantization or a second GPU. Throughput is excellent at roughly 27–30 tokens/sec thanks to the A100's bandwidth.

faq.q: Is Q8_0 worth it over Q6_K for 70B?
faq.a: At 70B the difference is marginal — Q6_K is already near-lossless. Q8_0 mainly makes sense when you have datacenter memory to spare and want a single canonical checkpoint.

faq.q: How much context fits alongside Q8 weights?
faq.a: About 4K–6K tokens at FP16 KV cache. With KV cache at Q8 you can roughly double that before hitting the 80GB ceiling.

faq.q: Would Q4 on the same A100 be better?
faq.a: It would free about 37 GB for a 128K+ context or much larger batches. For throughput-oriented serving with concurrent users, Q4 with a large KV cache usually beats Q8 with a tiny one.

pages.h1: Claude Sonnet vs GPT-4o: API Cost at Your Volume
pages.title: Claude Sonnet vs GPT-4o API Cost Calculator
pages.description: Compare Claude Sonnet 4 and GPT-4o token pricing: $3/$15 versus $2.50/$10 per million tokens, plus prompt caching savings at your real request volume.
pages.intro: Claude Sonnet 4 lists at $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens. GPT-4o lists at $2.50 and $10. Prompt caching changes the picture: Anthropic discounts cached input by 90% to $0.30, while OpenAI discounts to $1.25 — a 50% saving.
pages.verdict: For a chat product with 1,500 input and 800 output tokens per request at 2,000 requests/day, GPT-4o is roughly 30% cheaper before caching, but Sonnet pulls ahead on long system prompts where its 90% cache discount applies. Enter your own numbers above to see which side of the crossover you land on.

faq.q: Which model is cheaper for long system prompts?
faq.a: Anthropic's cache discount is 90% versus OpenAI's 50%, so with a 4K+ static system prompt and high cache hit rates, Sonnet's effective input cost can fall below GPT-4o's despite the higher list price.

faq.q: Does the calculator include batch discounts?
faq.a: No. Batch APIs typically halve the price for asynchronous work. Both providers offer one; apply roughly 50% to the token costs shown here if your workload is batchable.

faq.q: Are output tokens really 3–5× the input price?
faq.a: Yes, on both providers. Output dominates cost for chat and generation, so capping max output tokens and using structured output are the highest-leverage cost controls.

pages.h1: Gemini Flash API Cost for High-Volume Apps
pages.title: Gemini Flash API Pricing Estimator — High-Volume Workloads
pages.description: Gemini 1.5 Flash costs $0.075 per million input and $0.30 per million output tokens. Estimate monthly spend at 10k–500k requests per day.
pages.intro: Gemini 1.5 Flash is priced at $0.075 per million input tokens and $0.30 per million output tokens, with cached input at $0.019. At 100,000 requests per day with 800 input and 400 output tokens, the arithmetic lands in the low hundreds of dollars per month rather than the thousands.
pages.verdict: Flash is the cheapest mainstream multimodal tier and the right default for classification, extraction and tagging at volume. The constraint is quality ceiling, not price: validate accuracy on your task before routing production traffic to it.

faq.q: How much does 1 million Gemini Flash requests cost?
faq.a: At 800 input and 400 output tokens per request, about $180 for the million requests before caching. Cached input at $0.019 per million tokens can cut the input side by roughly 75%.

faq.q: Is the 1M context window priced differently?
faq.a: Google applies a higher per-token rate above 200K input tokens on some Gemini models. This calculator assumes the standard tier; long-context work should add a margin.

faq.q: When should I use Flash instead of Pro?
faq.a: Use Flash when the task is well-specified — extraction, routing, classification, short summaries. Move to Pro when reasoning depth or instruction fidelity matters more than the 8–10× price difference.

pages.h1: GPT-4o mini vs DeepSeek V3: Token Cost Comparison
pages.title: GPT-4o mini vs DeepSeek V3 API Cost Calculator
pages.description: GPT-4o mini is $0.15/$0.60 per million tokens; DeepSeek V3 is $0.27/$1.10. Compare monthly burn at 20,000 requests per day with caching.
pages.intro: GPT-4o mini lists at $0.15 input and $0.60 output per million tokens. DeepSeek V3 lists at $0.27 and $1.10 but delivers quality closer to a mid-tier flagship, which is why the comparison is rarely decided on price alone.
pages.verdict: On pure tokens, GPT-4o mini is roughly 40% cheaper. DeepSeek V3 typically replaces a larger model rather than a mini, so the fair comparison is against GPT-4o — where V3 is 8–9× cheaper. Model the task you actually run, not the tier label.

faq.q: Does DeepSeek cache prompts?
faq.a: Yes, with a 74% discount on cache hits ($0.07 per million tokens on V3). Cache hits require an identical prompt prefix, so structure prompts with static content first.

faq.q: What about latency and rate limits?
faq.a: DeepSeek's public API has historically been slower and more congested than OpenAI's. If you need predictable p95 latency, budget for a fallback provider or self-host V3.

faq.q: Is DeepSeek V3 open weights?
faq.a: Yes, which means you can self-host it — but at 671B parameters the hardware cost dwarfs API pricing for almost all workloads.

pages.h1: Claude Opus 4 API Cost Estimator
pages.title: Claude Opus 4 API Cost Calculator ($15 / $75 per Million Tokens)
pages.description: Claude Opus 4 costs $15 per million input and $75 per million output tokens. Estimate monthly spend for agentic and reasoning-heavy workloads.
pages.intro: Claude Opus 4 sits at $15 per million input and $75 per million output tokens, with cached input at $1.50. At 500 requests per day with 4,000 input and 2,000 output tokens, the monthly bill lands in the high hundreds before any caching.
pages.verdict: Opus is 5× Sonnet's price and only worth it on tasks where a wrong answer costs more than the tokens. The biggest lever is output length: at $75 per million, an extra 1,000 output tokens per request adds more cost than doubling your input.

faq.q: How do I cut Opus costs without switching models?
faq.a: Cache the system prompt and any retrieved documents (90% input discount), cap output with strict max_tokens, and route easy requests to Sonnet or Haiku with a classifier.

faq.q: Is extended thinking billed as output?
faq.a: Yes — thinking tokens are billed at the output rate. Long reasoning traces can multiply output cost, so measure actual usage rather than assuming the visible answer length.

faq.q: When is Opus actually cheaper overall?
faq.a: When it succeeds in one pass where a cheaper model needs three retries plus human review. Price per successful task, not price per token, is the correct comparison.

pages.h1: Customer Support Chatbot API Cost Calculator
pages.title: AI Support Chatbot Cost Per Month — Token Calculator
pages.description: Model the API cost of a support chatbot: 5,000 conversations per day, 900 input and 250 output tokens, with 60% prompt cache hit rate.
pages.intro: Support bots are input-heavy: a static policy prompt, a retrieved knowledge-base chunk and the conversation history all count as input, while answers stay short. That makes prompt caching the dominant cost control, not output trimming.
pages.verdict: At 5,000 conversations per day with 900 input and 250 output tokens, a budget model like Gemini Flash costs well under $100 per month, while a flagship model lands in the low thousands. Cache the policy and KB preamble and the input side drops by more than half.

faq.q: How many tokens is a typical support conversation?
faq.a: Single-turn answers run 600–1,200 input tokens with a retrieved KB chunk. Multi-turn threads grow linearly, so summarize history after 6–8 turns instead of resending it.

faq.q: Should I use one model for everything?
faq.a: No. A cheap model handles FAQ and intent routing; escalate to a stronger model only for refunds, technical troubleshooting or low-confidence cases. This typically cuts spend 60–80%.

faq.q: How do cache hits work in practice?
faq.a: Providers cache a stable prefix for minutes to hours. Put instructions and documents first, then the variable question last, and keep the prefix byte-identical between requests.

pages.h1: RAG Pipeline Token Cost Calculator
pages.title: RAG API Cost Calculator — Retrieval + Generation Tokens
pages.description: Estimate the monthly API cost of a RAG pipeline with 6,000 input tokens of retrieved context and 700 output tokens per query.
pages.intro: RAG requests are dominated by retrieved context. Six 500-token chunks plus a question put you near 6,000 input tokens per query, and that context is largely identical across queries against the same document set — an ideal caching candidate.
pages.verdict: At 8,000 queries per day with 6,000 input and 700 output tokens, input cost is 60–80% of the bill. Two levers matter: rerank and trim retrieved chunks to 3–4, and cache the shared document preamble where the provider supports it.

faq.q: How many chunks should I retrieve?
faq.a: Three to five after reranking. Going from eight chunks to four roughly halves input tokens with little quality loss when the reranker is good.

faq.q: Does caching help RAG if every query differs?
faq.a: Yes, if the cached prefix is your instructions plus a shared document set. Per-query retrieved chunks sit after the cached prefix and are billed normally.

faq.q: Should I use a smaller model for RAG?
faq.a: Usually yes. RAG quality is bounded by retrieval; a strong mid-tier model with good context often beats a flagship with a cluttered context window.

pages.h1: Code Assistant API Cost Per Month
pages.title: AI Code Assistant API Cost Calculator (Coding Tokens)
pages.description: Coding workloads send large file contexts and receive long diffs. Estimate monthly API spend for 1,500 daily requests at 5,000 input and 1,200 output tokens.
pages.intro: Code assistance is token-hungry in both directions: a repository context and edit instructions run 4,000–8,000 input tokens, and the returned diff is often 1,000+ output tokens. Code tokenizes at roughly 3.2 characters per token, not 4, so the same file costs about 25% more than prose.
pages.verdict: At 1,500 requests per day with 5,000 input and 1,200 output tokens, a mid-tier model costs a few hundred dollars a month while a flagship exceeds a thousand. Sending only the relevant file slice, rather than the whole repository, is the single biggest saving.

faq.q: Why do code prompts use more tokens per character?
faq.a: Identifiers, punctuation and indentation break into many small tokens. Expect about 3.2 characters per token for code versus 4 for English prose, so always use the code multiplier in the tokenizer above.

faq.q: Is prompt caching effective for coding agents?
faq.a: Very. An agent re-sends the same file context across many tool calls, so a stable cached prefix with a 90% discount can cut input cost by more than half.

faq.q: How do I cap runaway output cost?
faq.a: Set a hard max_tokens per edit, require unified diffs instead of full files, and reject responses that exceed a diff-size budget before they are applied.

pages.h1: DeepSeek R1 Reasoning Token Cost Calculator
pages.title: DeepSeek R1 API Cost — Reasoning Token Estimator
pages.description: Reasoning models bill hidden thinking tokens as output. Estimate R1 cost at 4,000 output tokens per request and compare with Claude and OpenAI.
pages.intro: DeepSeek R1 is cheap on paper at $0.55 input and $2.19 output per million tokens, but reasoning models emit thousands of hidden tokens before the visible answer. A request that looks like 500 output tokens can bill 4,000.
pages.verdict: Even with 4,000 output tokens per request, R1 at 1,000 requests per day stays in the low hundreds of dollars per month — several times cheaper than an equivalent Opus or o-series workload. Validate the actual reasoning-token count from your provider's usage field before committing to a budget.

faq.q: Are reasoning tokens billed as output?
faq.a: Yes on every major provider. The usage object reports them separately but the price is the output rate, which is why reasoning workloads cost far more than their visible answer length suggests.

faq.q: How many reasoning tokens should I budget per request?
faq.a: Measure it. Typical math and code tasks use 1,000–6,000 reasoning tokens; agentic planning can exceed 20,000. Set an internal reasoning budget and log the distribution.

faq.q: Does caching help reasoning models?
faq.a: Only on the input side. The reasoning trace itself is generated fresh each call, so cache the prompt and documents but expect no output-side discount.

pages.h1: Llama 3.3 70B API Cost: Hosted vs Self-Hosted
pages.title: Llama 3.3 70B API Cost Calculator — Hosted vs Self-Host
pages.description: Hosted Llama 3.3 70B runs about $0.59 per million input and $0.79 per million output tokens. Compare 15,000 daily requests against the cost of owning GPUs.
pages.intro: Llama 3.3 70B is available from multiple inference providers at roughly $0.59 per million input and $0.79 per million output tokens. Self-hosting the same model requires about 42 GB of VRAM at Q4, which means dual 24 GB cards or a single 48 GB workstation card.
pages.verdict: At 15,000 requests per day with 1,000 input and 600 output tokens, hosted inference costs a few hundred dollars a month. A dual-3090 rig costs several thousand up front plus power, so self-hosting only wins above roughly 10× that volume — or when data residency rules the API out.

faq.q: What hardware do I need to self-host Llama 3.3 70B?
faq.a: At Q4_K_M the weights are about 42 GB, so dual 24 GB GPUs or a 48 GB workstation card, plus roughly 1.5 GB of runtime overhead and KV cache for your context length.

faq.q: How many requests per day justify owning GPUs?
faq.a: As a rough break-even, several hundred thousand requests per day at these token counts. Below that, hosted pricing plus zero operations burden wins.

faq.q: Is hosted Llama pricing stable?
faq.a: No — inference providers compete aggressively and prices move. Treat the numbers here as a snapshot and re-run the comparison each quarter.

pages.h1: Can the RTX 3060 12GB Run Llama 3.3 70B at Q4_K_M?
pages.title: Llama 3.3 70B Q4_K_M on RTX 3060 12GB — VRAM, Speed & Fit
pages.description: Llama 3.3 70B at Q4_K_M needs ~43.4 GB with an 8K context; the RTX 3060 12GB offers 10.8 GB usable. Out of memory, ~1.3 tok/s.
pages.intro: Llama 3.3 70B Instruct at Q4_K_M, measured against the RTX 3060 12GB: weights, KV cache and runtime overhead versus 10.8 GB of usable VRAM.
pages.verdict: No. It needs about 43.4 GB against 10.8 GB usable — 32.6 GB short at an 8K context; the RTX A6000 48GB would fit. What runs well here instead: DeepSeek R1 7B at Q8_0.
pages.summary: The subject is Llama 3.3 70B Instruct, Meta's 70-billion-parameter dense instruction model and the strongest openly licensed generalist in its class for chat, tool calling and multilingual work, measured against the RTX 3060 12GB. In practice the target workload is a private general-purpose assistant or agent backend. Budget 43.4 GB before anything is generated — 39.4 GB for Q4_K_M weights, 2.50 GB for the KV cache across 8K tokens, and 1.5 GB of fixed overhead. For Llama 3.3 70B, the RTX 3060 12GB contributes 12 GB of VRAM, leaving about 10.8 GB for weights, cache and activations. That overshoots usable memory by 32.6 GB, so only about 25% of the model stays on the GPU and the rest spills to system RAM over PCIe. Decoding is memory-bandwidth bound, so expect roughly 1.3 tokens per second, which is too slow for interactive use. The largest model in this set that does run comfortably on the RTX 3060 12GB is DeepSeek R1 7B at Q8_0, at about 27 tokens per second — a far better use of this machine. No quantization in our table fits at this context, so the realistic upgrade is the RTX A6000 48GB or larger. pages.intro: Qwen 2.5 Coder 32B Instruct at Q8_0, measured against the RTX 5090 32GB: weights, KV cache and runtime overhead versus 28.8 GB of usable VRAM.
pages.verdict: No. It needs about 37.2 GB against 28.8 GB usable — 8.4 GB short at a 16K context; Q5_K_M would fit. What runs well here instead: DeepSeek R1 32B at Q4_K_M.
pages.summary: Short answer for Qwen 2.5 Coder 32B at Q8_0 on the RTX 5090 32GB: no. On the RTX 5090 32GB, the question is whether Qwen 2.5 Coder 32B Instruct — Alibaba's code-specialised 32B model, which scores close to frontier hosted models on code generation and repair benchmarks — can stay in memory. At Q8_0 (8.50 bits per weight) its weights occupy 31.7 GB, and a 16K-token context adds 4.00 GB of KV cache, for roughly 37.2 GB including the 1.5 GB runtime reserve. The RTX 5090 32GB provides 32 GB of VRAM, of which about 28.8 GB is realistically usable by Qwen 2.5 Coder 32B. That overshoots usable memory by 8.4 GB, so only about 77% of the model stays on the GPU and the rest spills to system RAM over PCIe. Decoding is memory-bandwidth bound, so expect roughly 25 tokens per second, which feels comfortably interactive. The largest model in this set that does run comfortably on the RTX 5090 32GB is DeepSeek R1 32B at Q4_K_M, at about 53 tokens per second — a far better use of this machine. Dropping to Q5_K_M would bring it inside the limit at this context, at some cost in output quality. For a local coding assistant wired into an editor, this is a non-starter without a different quantization or more memory.

faq.a: None at this quantization — the weights alone exceed the 28.8 GB of usable memory, so a smaller quantization or more memory is required before context even enters the picture.

pages.h1: Can the RTX 3060 12GB Run Mistral Large 2 at Q4_K_M?
pages.title: Mistral Large 2 Q4_K_M on RTX 3060 12GB — VRAM, Speed & Fit
pages.description: Mistral Large 2 at Q4_K_M needs ~73.4 GB with an 8K context; the RTX 3060 12GB offers 10.8 GB usable. Out of memory, ~under 1 tok/s.

pages.verdict: No. It needs about 73.4 GB against 10.8 GB usable — 62.6 GB short at an 8K context; the H100 80GB would fit. What runs well here instead: DeepSeek R1 7B at Q8_0.
pages.summary: Short answer for Mistral Large 2 at Q4_K_M on the RTX 3060 12GB: no. On the RTX 3060 12GB, the question is whether Mistral Large 2 (123B) — Mistral's 123-billion-parameter dense flagship, one of the largest open-weight models people seriously attempt to run outside a data centre — can stay in memory. At Q4_K_M (4.83 bits per weight) its weights occupy 69.2 GB, and an 8K-token context adds 2.75 GB of KV cache, for roughly 73.4 GB including the 1.5 GB runtime reserve. The RTX 3060 12GB provides 12 GB of VRAM, of which about 10.8 GB is realistically usable by Mistral Large 2. That overshoots usable memory by 62.6 GB, so only about 15% of the model stays on the GPU and the rest spills to system RAM over PCIe. Decoding is memory-bandwidth bound, so expect roughly under 1 tokens per second, which is too slow for interactive use. The largest model in this set that does run comfortably on the RTX 3060 12GB is DeepSeek R1 7B at Q8_0, at about 27 tokens per second — a far better use of this machine. No quantization in our table fits at this context, so the realistic upgrade is the H100 80GB or larger. For frontier-class quality on private hardware, this is a non-starter without a different quantization or more memory.
